case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates an implied private federal cause of action allowing private plaintiffs to sue for rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially § 80a-46(b)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action for rescission. They contend that under this Court’s modern implied-rights jurisprudence, a private remedy exists only when Congress clearly indicated an intent to create one through rights-creating statutory text and structure. In their view, Section 47(b) is primarily a remedial/contract-validity provision that specifies the legal effect of illegality and the availability of rescission when a proper plaintiff and cause of action already exist, rather than affirmatively authorizing private parties to file suit. Petitioners further emphasize that the ICA contains an express private right of action in another provision (commonly cited in this context as Section 36(b)), suggesting Congress knew how to authorize private suits and chose not to do so in Section 47(b). They warn that recognizing an implied rescission action would invite opportunistic shareholder/activist litigation and expand liability beyond what Congress authorized, even if the remedy is formally framed as rescission rather than damages.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plain text of Section 47(b)(2) affirmatively contemplates rescission being sought by parties to an illegal contract and therefore authorizes a private cause of action (at least for the limited remedy of rescission/voiding and restitutionary relief). They rely on the statutory language as 'rights-creating' in the sense that it identifies who may obtain rescission and under what circumstances, and they argue that this Court’s precedent (including decisions discussing contract-voiding provisions in related securities statutes) supports a limited private remedy to unwind unlawful contracts even if broader damages remedies are unavailable. Respondents also contend that any circuit disagreement is narrow or underdeveloped and that, in practice, Section 47(b) rescission claims are relatively uncommon and limited in scope (not a backdoor to compensatory damages), reducing the policy concerns asserted by petitioners and amici.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. (TAMA) v. Lewis, 444 U.S. 11 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that §47(b)(2)’s “at the instance of any party” is the respondents’ best textual hook, because it sounds like a party can come to court and request rescission. But as Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas emphasize, Sandoval requires clear congressional intent to create a private cause of action, and court-directed remedial language can just as naturally function as a rule of decision once a case is properly before a court (including defensively or within an independently authorized claim). The broader ICA enforcement architecture—SEC-centered enforcement with an express, targeted private action in §36(b)—makes it implausible that Congress silently created an additional, freestanding private rescission suit through contract-validity language. Transamerica, predating our modern implied-rights framework, cannot supply the missing clear authorization in this statutory design.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s argument that §47(b)(2) “presupposes” a private suit because it says a court may not deny rescission at a party’s instance mistakes a remedial limitation for an affirmative cause of action. Under Sandoval, we must find congressional intent to create both a private right and a private remedy; language regulating what a court may do once properly seized of a case does not itself confer a legal right to hale a defendant into federal court. As the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan observe, the ICA’s structure—especially Congress’s express creation of a private action in §36(b) amid an SEC-centered enforcement scheme—strongly indicates Congress did not mean §47(b) to be a freestanding private enforcement mechanism. Section 47(b) can still do work as a rule of decision (including in defensive postures or within an independently authorized action), but it does not supply the cause of action respondents need.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right that §47(b)(2)’s phrase “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” is the respondents’ best textual hook, because it sounds like a party may affirmatively request relief. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval requires evidence that Congress intended to create not just a remedy but a freestanding private cause of action, and court-directed remedial instructions can operate simply as a rule of decision once some proper action is already before the court. The ICA’s overall design—SEC-centered enforcement plus an express, carefully cabined private action in §36(b)—is powerful contextual evidence that Congress did not silently authorize a broad additional private enforcement suit through §47(b). Transamerica, for the reasons Justice Kagan and Justice Thomas give, cannot supply the missing clarity after our modern intent-focused framework and materially different statutory context.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I take Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s point that §47(b)(2) can be characterized as merely remedial—telling a court what it may do once a case is properly before it—and that the ICA’s express private action in §36(b) reflects calibrated enforcement. But Sandoval asks whether Congress intended a private remedy, and §47(b)(2)’s directive—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—is not just a generic remedial menu; it is a court-facing command keyed to a party’s invocation, which is difficult to reconcile with the view that no party may ever affirmatively seek that relief. The structure cuts both ways: Congress’s choice to specify a narrow, contract-centered rescission obligation here can complement SEC enforcement without creating the broader damages regime my colleagues fear. Put differently, calling §47(b) a “rule of decision” does not explain why Congress spoke in mandatory, party-invoking terms that make most sense if unlawful ICA contracts are rescindable in a party-initiated action.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that §47(b)(2)’s phrase “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” sounds like it anticipates a party seeking rescission. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, that is most naturally read as a remedial constraint—a rule about what a court may do once a properly authorized claim is before it—rather than the kind of rights-creating, defendant-naming authorization Sandoval requires to infer a freestanding private cause of action. The ICA’s broader enforcement design matters here: Congress knew how to create a private suit and did so expressly in §36(b), while otherwise relying on SEC-centered enforcement, which strongly counsels against treating §47(b) as silently “adding” a new private enforcement mechanism. Transamerica cannot supply the missing clear statement, both because it predates our modern implied-right framework and because importing its approach would override the ICA’s calibrated scheme.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press the textual hook in §47(b)(2)—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—because it sounds like an affirmative request for relief. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Sandoval requires clear congressional creation of a cause of action, and court-directed remedial instructions can function as rules of decision once a case is properly before a court (including defensively or within an expressly authorized suit) without themselves authorizing anyone to hale a defendant into federal court. The ICA’s structure reinforces that reading: Congress knew how to create a private action when it wished (e.g., §36(b)) and otherwise relied heavily on SEC-centered enforcement, which counsels against "raising up" a new freestanding private rescission action from contract-validity language. Transamerica, predating our modern clear-statement approach, cannot supply the missing rights-creating clarity in §47(b).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s strongest point is textual: §47(b)(2) says a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party,” which can sound like an invitation to file an affirmative suit. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize, Sandoval requires clear congressional creation of a private cause of action, and court-directed remedial language more naturally presupposes an already-valid vehicle for suit and then constrains the remedy once the court is properly seized. The ICA’s enforcement architecture—SEC-centered, with an expressly created and carefully limited private action in §36(b)—is powerful contextual evidence against silently “adding” a broad private rescission action via §47(b). Section 47(b) can still function as a rule of decision about illegality and rescission within authorized litigation (or defensively) without implying a freestanding private right to sue.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press the textual force of §47(b)(2)’s phrase “a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party,” which sounds like it anticipates a party asking for rescission. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, Sandoval requires evidence that Congress created a private cause of action—not merely that it regulated the availability of a remedy once a court is properly engaged—and §47(b) reads more naturally as a remedial limitation/rule of decision rather than rights-creating authorization to sue. The ICA’s structure, including the Act’s SEC-centered enforcement and Congress’s decision to confer an express private right in §36(b) but not generally elsewhere, is strong contextual evidence against implying a freestanding private rescission action from §47(b). Section 47(b) can still have meaningful work to do (including as a defense or as a remedy within an action brought under an express cause of action) without transforming it into an implied private enforcement mechanism.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor is right to press that §47(b)(2)’s “at the instance of any party” sounds like party-initiated litigation, not merely an abstract remedial directive. But as Justice Kagan and the Chief explain, Sandoval requires an unambiguous congressional creation of a private right and remedy, and court-directed limits on denying rescission more naturally operate as a rule of decision once a case is properly before the court, not as an affirmative authorization to sue. The ICA’s structure—particularly Congress’s express choice to create a specific private action in §36(b) within an otherwise SEC-centered scheme—makes it implausible that Congress silently added a broad, freestanding rescission cause of action via §47(b). Transamerica cannot supply the missing clarity under our modern implied-rights framework, and §47(b) still has meaningful work to do without being transformed into an implied private enforcement mechanism.

John Roberts.reasoning: Beginning with Congress’s enforcement design, the Investment Company Act largely channels compliance through SEC oversight and specified enforcement mechanisms, and when Congress meant to authorize private plaintiffs it did so expressly (as in § 36(b)), which strongly suggests § 47(b) is remedial rather than rights-creating. Under our modern implied-rights cases, the question is not whether rescission is a familiar remedy but whether the statute’s text and structure clearly manifest congressional intent to create a private cause of action; § 47(b)(2)’s direction about when a court may grant rescission presupposes an existing cause of action rather than supplying one. Respondents’ reliance on Transamerica is misplaced because that decision predated Sandoval’s stricter approach and rested on materially different statutory language in the Investment Advisers Act’s contract-voiding provision. Absent clear textual authorization, we should not infer a new private federal cause of action that Congress did not create, particularly given the Act’s calibrated remedial scheme.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Sandoval, the judicial task is to determine whether Congress intended to create both a private right and a private remedy; absent that intent, courts may not manufacture a cause of action. Section 47(b) speaks in remedial/contract-validity terms—describing when an ICA-violative contract is unenforceable and when rescission may be appropriate—without expressly authorizing any private party to sue, which is a strong indication Congress did not create a freestanding private cause of action. The Investment Company Act’s structure reinforces that conclusion because Congress elsewhere provided an express private action (e.g., §36(b)), showing it knew how to confer a private remedy when it wished and declined to do so in §47(b). Whatever rescission may be available through historically recognized equitable principles in a properly brought action, §47(b) itself does not create the necessary legal right to relief in federal court.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Alexander v. Sandoval, the dispositive question is whether §47(b) displays congressional intent to create not only a private right but also a private remedy. Section 47(b) is framed as a contract-validity and remedial directive—specifying the legal consequences of illegality and when rescission is “available”—but it does not use rights-creating language that authorizes private plaintiffs to file suit, especially against the backdrop of the ICA’s enforcement scheme that elsewhere provides express private actions (e.g., §36(b)) while generally entrusting enforcement to the SEC. Treating §47(b)(2)’s reference to rescission as itself creating a freestanding federal cause of action would dilute Sandoval by inferring a remedy from something less than a clear indication that Congress meant to confer one. Nor is Transamerica (TAMA) an adequate analogue here, because it turned on materially different statutory text and context, and we should not extend it to create a significant new private enforcement mechanism absent clearer congressional direction.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Under Sandoval, the question is whether §47(b) displays an intent to create not just a private right but also a private remedy, and §47(b)(2)’s text does: it speaks in remedial, court-directed terms (“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”) and thus presupposes that a party to an unlawful ICA contract may invoke a judicial remedy to unwind it. Structurally, that mandatory limitation on judicial discretion functions like a money-mandating/relief-mandating command: once an ICA-violative contract and the relevant equities are shown, the statute dictates the availability of rescission (and associated restitution), which is strong textual evidence Congress intended a limited private remedial vehicle rather than mere contract “illegality” rhetoric. Petitioners’ reliance on the ICA’s express private action elsewhere does not overcome this text, because §47(b) is not a freewheeling enforcement provision but a targeted remedial mechanism tied to specific unlawful contracts, complementing SEC enforcement rather than displacing it. This reading also aligns with the Court’s treatment of materially similar contract-voiding language as supporting a limited private rescission remedy in the paired 1940 Acts context.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Section 47(b) speaks to the legal status of contracts made or performed in violation of the Act and to the availability of rescission as a remedy, but it does not anywhere clearly authorize a private party to file suit in federal court to obtain that relief. Under our modern approach, the question is not whether rescission would be sensible policy, but whether Congress unmistakably created a cause of action—and here the Act’s structure cuts the other way, because when Congress wanted private enforcement it said so expressly (as in §36(b)) and otherwise lodged enforcement authority with the SEC. Reading §47(b)(2) as creating a freestanding private rescission action would bypass that enforcement scheme and convert a remedial/contract-validity provision into an implied right to sue without the clear textual signal Sandoval requires. Whatever TAMA may have inferred from different statutory language in a different statute, it cannot overcome the ICA’s text and design, which do not make Congress’s intent to authorize private suits “any clearer.”

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Sandoval, a private cause of action must be created by Congress, and we look for clear, unambiguous rights-creating language with an unmistakable focus on the individual plaintiff. Section 47(b) largely speaks in remedial and structural terms—addressing the legal effect of an unlawful contract and directing when a court may deny rescission—without affirmatively authorizing any class of private plaintiffs to sue in the first place. The ICA’s express private action in §36(b) reinforces that Congress knew how to provide investor suits when it wished, and its broader enforcement architecture (SEC oversight and other specified mechanisms) counsels against judicially “raising up” an additional rescission action. Whatever TAMA said about a parallel IAA provision, it predates (and cannot overcome) the modern, stringent clarity requirement, and in any event §47(b)’s text still does not supply the necessary rights-creating cause-of-action grant.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under this Court’s modern implied-rights cases, the question is whether Congress clearly created a private cause of action in the text and structure of the ICA; Section 47(b) reads as a remedial/contract-validity rule (what follows if a contract violates the Act), not an affirmative, rights-creating authorization for private plaintiffs to file suit. The ICA’s broader enforcement architecture reinforces that conclusion: Congress expressly provided limited private enforcement in provisions such as Section 36(b) while otherwise relying primarily on SEC enforcement, which is strong evidence that Congress did not intend an additional implied rescission action in Section 47(b). Respondents’ reliance on the “void” language and Transamerica is weakened because Transamerica predates Sandoval’s strict approach and, in any event, a voidness provision can have work to do as a rule of decision (including defensively or within otherwise-proper suits) without creating a new freestanding federal cause of action. Recognizing an implied private right here would improperly convert a statutory remedial consequence into an implied private enforcement mechanism Congress did not clearly authorize.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Applying ordinary interpretive tools, §47(b) speaks in remedial, contract-validity terms (what happens to an unlawful contract and what relief a court may award) but does not use rights-creating language that affirmatively authorizes a private plaintiff to file suit in federal court. The ICA’s structure reinforces that conclusion: Congress provided express private enforcement in limited, specified provisions (notably §36(b), and other targeted private-suit authorizations), while otherwise relying on SEC enforcement and a detailed regulatory scheme—context that is difficult to square with implying a broad, freestanding rescission action under §47(b). Under this Court’s modern implied-rights cases, the presence of such alternative and comprehensive enforcement mechanisms is powerful evidence that Congress did not intend to create additional private litigation beyond what it expressly provided. Section 47(b) therefore supplies a remedy only when a proper cause of action exists elsewhere; it does not itself create a private federal cause of action for rescission of contracts alleged to violate the Act.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Using the traditional tools of statutory construction, Section 47(b) reads as a contract-validity/remedial provision that specifies the consequence of an ICA violation (voidability and possible rescission) rather than unambiguously conferring on private parties an affirmative right to sue in federal court. Section 47(b)(2)’s description of when a court may grant rescission does not supply the clear, rights-creating textual signal or express cause-of-action language that this Court’s modern implied-rights cases require, and it is not enough that respondents are within the statute’s protective purposes. The ICA’s structure reinforces that conclusion because Congress elsewhere provided express, “by-its-terms limited” private enforcement mechanisms (e.g., § 36(b)), which counsels against implying an additional private rescission action from § 47(b) absent clear authorization. Treating § 47(b) as an implied cause of action would improperly use a remedial/waiver-like provision to silently expand the universe of substantive claims beyond what Congress created.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates an implied private federal cause of action allowing private plaintiffs to seek rescission of contracts that allegedly violate the Act.
case_analysis.legal_provision: Investment Company Act of 1940, Section 47(b), 15 U.S.C. § 80a-46(b) (especially § 47(b)(2)).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that ICA § 47(b) does not authorize private parties to sue in federal court for rescission. In their view, § 47(b) is a remedial/contract-validity provision that specifies the consequences of illegality when a proper enforcement action exists, but it does not itself create a 'rights-creating' private right or a private cause of action. They emphasize the Supreme Court’s modern approach (e.g., Sandoval) requiring clear textual and structural evidence of congressional intent to create a private remedy, and contend that the ICA’s detailed enforcement scheme (centered on SEC enforcement and a small number of express private rights elsewhere in the ICA) would be undermined by implying an additional, broad rescission remedy. Petitioners and supporting amici also stress that allowing private rescission suits would invite strategic, self-interested litigation in the registered-fund space and effectively create an end-run around the limits on private enforcement Congress chose.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue that the plain text of § 47(b)(2) authorizes parties to an illegal ICA contract to seek rescission and related restitutionary relief. They contend that the provision’s language and structure reflect congressional intent to permit private litigants to unwind unlawful contracts—at least to obtain the traditional equitable remedy of rescission (not compensatory damages). Respondents rely on the idea that when Congress declares certain contracts unlawful/void (or unenforceable), it commonly contemplates judicial rescission at the behest of injured parties, and they maintain that this case fits within that tradition. They further argue that the Second Circuit’s interpretation aligns with statutory text and that policy objections or broader 'contemporary legal context' arguments cannot overcome what they characterize as § 47(b)(2)’s straightforward remedial direction.
key_precedents: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. Transport Workers Union of America, 451 U.S. 77 (1981)
Transamerica Mortgage Advisors, Inc. v. Lewis (TAMA), 444 U.S. 11 (1979)
Touche Ross & Co. v. Redington, 442 U.S. 560 (1979)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s strongest point remains that §47(b)(2) speaks in remedial terms—“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”—which sounds like it contemplates a litigant invoking a court’s power. But as Justice Thomas and Justice Barrett emphasize, Sandoval makes clear that remedial, court-directed language does not itself supply the antecedent cause of action; it can operate as a rule governing the availability of rescission once a dispute is properly before a court under some other source of authority. The ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s selective creation of express private rights elsewhere reinforce that we should not infer a freestanding private rescission action from this contract-validity provision. A narrow holding—limited to the absence of a private cause of action in §47(b) without revisiting Transamerica beyond distinguishing its text and pre-Sandoval context—should maintain the coalition.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best textual point is that §47(b)(2) specifies a remedy (rescission) and who may invoke it (“any party”), which can sound like an authorization to sue. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Alito explain, Sandoval requires enacted text showing Congress intended to create not only a remedy but also a private cause of action, and court-directed remedial language can “presuppose” litigation without supplying the antecedent claim-creating authorization. Read most naturally, §47(b) standardizes the remedial consequences of illegality once a dispute is properly before a court (including in SEC actions, defenses, or ancillary equitable proceedings), rather than silently reallocating enforcement authority from the SEC to private plaintiffs. The ICA’s SEC-centered structure and Congress’s choice to provide express private remedies elsewhere make it especially improper for us to imply a freestanding rescission action here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best point is textual: §47(b)(2) names a remedy (rescission) and says a court may not deny it “at the instance of any party,” which she argues presupposes a party’s ability to sue. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Sandoval requires more than remedial language that assumes litigation; we must find enacted text showing Congress intended to create a freestanding private cause of action, and §47(b) reads more naturally as a constraint on courts’ remedial discretion once a case is properly before them. The ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement structure, coupled with Congress’s decision to provide express private remedies in limited provisions, is powerful evidence against implying an additional private rescission action from contract-validity language. Transamerica, decided in a different statutory setting and before our modern implied-rights framework, cannot supply the missing congressional intent to create a private remedy enforceable by suit here.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right that §47(b)(2)’s “at the instance of any party” language most naturally envisions a litigant requesting rescission, and that feature makes the respondent’s textual case the hardest to dismiss. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, Sandoval draws a firm line between identifying a remedy and creating a freestanding cause of action, and §47(b) is framed as a limitation on courts’ remedial discretion once rescission is otherwise properly sought, not as rights-creating, plaintiff-focused authorization to sue. Reading §47(b) to silently create a new private rescission action would also sit uneasily with the ICA’s comprehensive, SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s selective decision to provide express private rights elsewhere—structural signals that counsel against implication here. On this view, §47(b) still does substantial work as a federal rule of decision governing rescission in cases properly before the court (including SEC actions and defensive/ancillary rescission) without reallocating enforcement authority from the SEC to private plaintiffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I take seriously the Chief Justice’s and Justice Thomas’s point that, under Sandoval, remedial language aimed at courts does not automatically supply a freestanding cause of action. But §47(b)(2) is not framed as a general remedial “instruction” untethered to a litigant; it singles out who may invoke the remedy (“any party”) and then limits when a court may deny it, complete with enumerated exceptions—features that look like Congress designing a narrow equitable action rather than merely describing relief in some other, unspecified suit. The SEC-centered structure is real, as Justice Barrett stresses, yet it cuts both ways: Congress could rationally reserve damages and broad enforcement to the SEC while still permitting parties to unwind unlawful ICA contracts through rescission, and §47(b) is the statute’s specific mechanism for that. On balance, I do not think we can read “at the instance of any party” as doing no authorizing work at all without draining the provision of the clarity Sandoval seeks in identifying who may ask a federal court to act.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right that §47(b)(2) names both a remedy (rescission) and a requester (“any party”), and that is the best textual argument for an affirmative suit. But Sandoval teaches we must find enacted text creating a cause of action, not merely describing what remedies a court may award once a case is properly before it; as the Chief Justice underscores, court-directed remedial language can do real work without supplying the antecedent right to sue. Read in context, “at the instance of any party” functions naturally as a limitation on equitable discretion in cases brought under some other jurisdictional and claim-conferring source (including SEC enforcement or defensive rescission), rather than unmistakable rights-creating language. And the ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement structure—with select express private remedies elsewhere—reinforces that we should not “raise up” an additional private cause of action from §47(b)’s contract-validity/remedies provision.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s best textual point is that §47(b)(2) specifies both a remedy (rescission) and who may seek it (“any party”), which can sound like an invitation to sue. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas explain, under Sandoval/Gonzaga we must find enacted text creating a cause of action, and court-directed remedial limits can “presuppose” litigation while still operating only once a proper claim is otherwise before the court (including SEC enforcement or defensive/ancillary rescission). The ICA’s SEC-centered structure and Congress’s selective inclusion of express private remedies elsewhere make it especially implausible that §47(b) silently created a freestanding private rescission action. On that reading, §47(b) still does meaningful work as a uniform federal rule governing the availability of rescission without expanding judicial power beyond what Congress clearly authorized.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kagan’s textual point—§47(b)(2) names a remedy (rescission) and who may invoke it (“any party”)—is the strongest case for a private suit, because it sounds like a litigant-facing entitlement. But as the Chief Justice and Justice Thomas emphasize, Sandoval draws a sharp line between remedial instructions to courts and enacted text creating an antecedent private cause of action; §47(b) reads more naturally as limiting a court’s remedial discretion once rescission is otherwise properly in play, not as authorizing a freestanding federal claim. The ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement design and Congress’s selective creation of express private remedies elsewhere make it implausible that §47(b) silently reallocates enforcement authority to private plaintiffs. On this reading, §47(b) still does real work as a federal rule of decision about the effect of illegality in contracts without requiring us to “create” a cause of action Congress did not clearly provide.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kagan is right that §47(b)(2)’s reference to rescission “at the instance of any party” is the best textual hook for Respondent, because it contemplates a party requesting relief in court. But under Sandoval/Gonzaga, that kind of court-directed remedial instruction is not an “unambiguous conferral” of a privately enforceable right or a freestanding cause of action; as the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett emphasize, it can instead operate as a limitation on courts’ discretion once a case is properly before them under some other claim or posture. The ICA’s SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s selective creation of express private remedies elsewhere make it implausible to treat §47(b) as silently reallocating enforcement authority to private plaintiffs. On this reading, §47(b) still does real work—standardizing the availability of rescission when illegality is established—without crossing the distinct, text-dependent threshold for creating a new private suit.

John Roberts.reasoning: The starting point is the statutory scheme Congress enacted in the Investment Company Act: it assigns primary enforcement authority to the SEC and, when Congress wished to authorize private enforcement, it did so expressly in limited provisions—strong structural evidence against implying an additional, freestanding private cause of action for rescission in §47(b). The text of §47(b)(2) (“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party” absent specified conditions) is naturally read as a remedial rule governing the availability of rescission once a party is properly in court—e.g., as a defense or in an action brought under an existing cause of action—not as rights-creating language that itself authorizes private plaintiffs to sue. Under this Court’s modern approach, we do not infer private remedies without clear textual and structural indication of congressional intent, and implying one here would circumvent the enforcement design Congress chose. Transamerica does not compel a different result because it turned on materially different statutory language in a different statute and, in any event, predates the stricter interpretive approach reaffirmed in Sandoval.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Under Sandoval, the question is whether §47(b)’s enacted text and structure show Congress intended to create both a private right in the plaintiff class and a private remedy enforceable by private suit. Section 47(b) is a contract-validity/remedial directive (“a court may not deny rescission at the instance of any party”) that presupposes a proper cause of action; it does not contain the rights-creating language that focuses on protecting a particular class, and it does not confer an affirmative entitlement to sue. That reading is reinforced by the ICA’s detailed, SEC-centered enforcement scheme and Congress’s decision to provide express private remedies elsewhere, which counsels against judicially implying an additional rescission action here. Recognizing a free-standing private cause of action from §47(b) would therefore amount to courts “creat[ing] one” without the clear congressional intent Sandoval requires.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Sandoval, the dispositive question is whether §47(b) displays congressional intent to create not only a private right but also a private remedy (a cause of action) for private plaintiffs; it is not enough that the provision describes an entitlement to rescission in the abstract. Section 47(b)(2) speaks in remedial terms—directing what a “court may not deny” once rescission is sought—but it does not identify a class of protected plaintiffs or contain rights-creating language, and the ICA’s overall structure relies primarily on SEC enforcement with only limited express private remedies elsewhere, counseling against implying an additional one. Reading §47(b) to supply a freestanding private cause of action would therefore be an unwarranted expansion inconsistent with the Court’s general implied-right-of-action precedents. Whatever force Transamerica had in construing the IAA’s distinct provision, Sandoval’s intent-to-create-a-remedy requirement governs here and is not satisfied by §47(b)’s contract-validity language alone.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 47(b) is framed as a remedial rule governing the availability of rescission once a court is already properly exercising jurisdiction over a dispute; it does not, in text or structure, identify a class of private plaintiffs empowered to sue or otherwise supply the kind of rights-creating language that, under Sandoval, signals Congress’s intent to create a new freestanding federal cause of action. Read holistically within the ICA’s comprehensive enforcement design—where Congress expressly created limited private rights in specific provisions but otherwise assigned primary enforcement to the SEC—implying an additional, broadly available rescission suit would disrupt the statute’s calibrated allocation between private litigation and agency enforcement. The phrase that a court may not deny rescission “at the instance of any party” can do work as a federal rule of decision (including defensively or as ancillary equitable relief) without creating a standalone private right to file suit in federal court.
